newsitem.title: UK: British budget to boost gilts but trials ahead.
newsitem.headline: British budget to boost gilts but trials ahead.

text.p: British government securities may get a short-term lift from the 1997/98 budget being unveiled next week but interest rate jitters and political concerns will quickly return to vex the market, analysts said on Friday.

"Our best guess is the Chancellor (finance minister) will have some pleasant surprises for the market and we'll see a rally next week after the budget," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Investment Bank in London.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is set to present his 1997/1998 budget on Tuesday.
Analysts largely expect Clarke to resist the temptation to slash taxes in an effort to boost ruling Conservative Party chances before a general election polls due by May.
Instead, with last month's surprise interest rate rise bolstering his credentials as a fiscally responsible finance minister, they expect a cautious to neutral budget.

A survey of 27 economists conducted by Reuters forecast tax cuts of 2.25 billion sterling ($3.79 billion), to be offset by spending cuts. The public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) looks set to be trimmed to 26 billion sterling from 27 billion sterling this year.
"If it's a cautious budget and we don't see any significant tax cuts... gilts could actually benefit," Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London, said.
Coleman at CIBC said Clarke could slice a little more off the PSBR then the market is expecting in an effort to reduce the pressure for further rate increases.
"The best way he could do that is for him to introduce quite a tight budget and to ignore some of the more populist measures he might be tempted to introduce," he said.

Coleman said the 10-year gilt/Bund spread could contract to 170 basis points next week from around 180 now on the back of a cautious budget, though there was some risk budget optimism had already been taken for granted.
But analysts said the budget was not the main story for gilts in the weeks ahead. The focus would be on inflation, interest rates and sterling. Politics would be a side issue.

"The wider issue is still interest rates and whatever Mr Clarke does next week the market will still look for a rise in interest rates in December," said Coleman. "That will probably limit the upside for gilts."
The Bank of England raised interest rates one quarter point to 6.0 percent on October 30 but with consumers already spending eagerly and Christmas ahead, analysts say it will not stop there.
Shah sees the gilt/Bund gap pushing back out to around 200 basis points in the next couple of weeks and 10-year yields edging up to 7.75 to 8.00 percent from 7.47 percent now.
Gilts could also suffer if sterling's scorching rally pulls back, as some analysts expect, and investors take profits.
"At current levels on a spread basis, hedge your currency exposure," Shah said.

Rumbling in the background was unease in the gilt market over whether Prime Minister John Major could hang on to his wafer-thin one seat majority in the House of Commons with a by-election set for December. However the government could always muster support from other parties for key votes.

Analysts said gilts offered value on a relative basis against other European markets. Gilts could benefit if high yielders like Spain and Italy lost their lustre on any dimming of enthusiasm over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
"It is rather an absurd situation to have gilts the highest yielding market in Europe," said Doug Jones, senior investment manager at Gartmore, which manages $12 billion in fixed income.
Jones said the gilt/Bund gap has the potential to narrow to around 120 basis points once the election was out of the way.

"We probably have an excess political risk premium in the market at the moment and once you get a change to a new government, with presumably a working majority, then some of the risk premium will drop out," he said.
($1=.5937 Sterling)
